Agua Azul lies in Chiapas and is known for the turquoise-blue hues of its water. The cascades flow over rocky ledges, while surrounding vegetation forms a green backdrop to the river scenery. Both the individual streams and the overall succession of falls are worth seeing.

The waterfalls provide a natural stop on the road between San Cristóbal and Palenque. Along this route, mountainous areas gradually give way to wetter forest landscapes. Agua Azul offers a chance to linger by the river, explore the cascades and experience the changing scenery before visiting Maya archaeological complexes.

Agua Clara is located on the Caribbean side of the Panama Canal. The lock complex raises and lowers vessels between sea level and the inland waterway. Watching the process reveals how chambers and gates help large ships cross the isthmus.

From the visitor center, you can observe ship movements and the engineering works. Agua Clara adds a modern facility designed for large vessels to the story of the canal. It is fascinating to follow the stages of a ship passing through the locks and compare the size of the chambers with the vessels gradually moving between them.

Aguas Calientes, also known as Machu Picchu Pueblo, sits in a mountain valley near Machu Picchu. Trains arrive here, and travelers then continue to the archaeological complex. The town provides a convenient place to stay close to the monument and enjoy the landscape of high mountain slopes and lush vegetation.

Beyond a visit to Machu Picchu, the hot springs and craft market are also worth exploring. These attractions complement the ancient Inca city with a glimpse of modern life in the valley. After touring the archaeological complex, travelers return to the hotels, restaurants and railway station in Aguas Calientes.
